title: Powers of a regular sequence
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $M$ an $R$-module, $f_1,\dots,f_r\in R$ and $e_1,\dots,e_r>0$ integers. Then $f_1,\dots,f_r$ is an $M$-regular sequence [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence] if and only if $f_1^{e_1},\dots,f_r^{e_r}$ is an $M$-regular sequence.

proof.text: Reformulation of the definition [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence]. For an $R$-module $N$ and $g_1,\dots,g_s\in R$ ($s\ge0$) say that $g_1,\dots,g_s$ is *weakly $N$-regular* if condition (1) of the definition holds: $g_i$ is a nonzerodivisor on $N/(g_1,\dots,g_{i-1})N$ for $i=1,\dots,s$ (the empty sequence is weakly $N$-regular). Then $f_1,\dots,f_r$ is $M$-regular iff it is weakly $M$-regular and $M/(f_1,\dots,f_r)M\neq0$. Moreover, for $s\ge1$, $g_1,\dots,g_s$ is weakly $N$-regular iff $g_1$ is a nonzerodivisor on $N$ and $g_2,\dots,g_s$ is weakly $N/g_1N$-regular: for $2\le i\le s$ the $R$-modules $(N/g_1N)/(g_2,\dots,g_{i-1})(N/g_1N)$ and $N/(g_1,\dots,g_{i-1})N$ are equal (both are $N$ modulo $g_1N+g_2N+\dots+g_{i-1}N$), so multiplication by $g_i$ is the same map on both.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 07DV (lemma-regular-sequence-powers), proof (the reduction 'by induction applied to M/f_1M'); definition Tag 00LF

proof.text: One element. Let $N$ be an $R$-module, $f\in R$, $e\ge1$. (a) $f$ is a nonzerodivisor on $N$ iff $f^e$ is: if $f$ is one and $f^ex=0$, then $f\cdot f^{e-1}x=0$ gives $f^{e-1}x=0$, and by induction on $e$ $x=0$; if $f^e$ is one and $fx=0$, then $f^ex=f^{e-1}(fx)=0$, so $x=0$ (Stacks' facts (a) and (b)). (b) If $f$ is a nonzerodivisor on $N$ and $e\ge2$, then $0\to N/fN\xrightarrow{f^{e-1}}N/f^eN\to N/f^{e-1}N\to0$ is a short exact sequence of $R$-modules, where the first map sends $x\bmod fN$ to $f^{e-1}x\bmod f^eN$ (well defined as $f^{e-1}\cdot fN=f^eN$) and the second is the projection ($f^eN\subseteq f^{e-1}N$). Indeed the projection is surjective with kernel $f^{e-1}N/f^eN$, which is the image of the first map; and if $f^{e-1}x=f^ey$ then $f^{e-1}(x-fy)=0$, so $x=fy\in fN$ by (a), i.e. the first map is injective.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 07DV (lemma-regular-sequence-powers), proof (case r = 1, facts (a), (b); the short exact sequence with the map f_1^{e-1})

proof.text: Nonvanishing, proved without a monomial expansion. For a module N and element f, f^e N = N iff fN = N for e > 0: multiplication by f^e is an iterate of multiplication by f, and an iterate is surjective iff the map is. For a list f :: rs, quotient N first by (rs)N; the final quotient is zero iff multiplication by f on N/(rs)N is surjective. Mathlib Submodule.quotOfListConsSMulTopEquivQuotSMulTopOuter gives this identification. Hence changing just the head to a positive power preserves vanishing. Induct on list length, using Submodule.top_eq_ofList_cons_smul_iff to change the tail on N/fN, and then changing the head. This proves that the original and powered lists have nonzero final quotient simultaneously, including the empty list and zero module.

proof.text: Prove weak regularity ascends a short exact sequence directly in Lean. Induct on the tail list. Mathlib isSMulRegular_of_range_eq_ker transfers regularity of the head from the outer modules to the middle. Because the head is regular on the right, the snake-lemma consequence [lem-weil-pbc-snake-lemma-modules], implemented by QuotSMulTop.map_first_exact_on_four_term_exact_of_isSMulRegular_last applied to 0 -> A -> B -> C, proves injectivity after quotienting by the head. QuotSMulTop.map_exact and map_surjective preserve the other properties of the row. Apply list induction. Now induct on the positive exponent using the explicitly constructed row in Step 2: weak regularity of a tail on N/fN propagates to N/f^eN.

proof.text: Reflect weak regularity from B=N/f^eN to A=N/fN for e>=2. Use strong induction on the index i in the tail list rs. The preceding elements form a weakly regular prefix rs.take i on A by induction, and therefore also on C=N/f^(e-1)N by Step 4. The snake-lemma consequence [lem-weil-pbc-snake-lemma-modules], implemented by Mathlib map_first_exact_on_four_term_right_exact_of_isSMulRegular_last applied to the four-term exact sequence 0 -> A -> B -> C -> 0 and this prefix on C, makes the induced A/(rs.take i)A -> B/(rs.take i)B injective. The next element is regular on the latter quotient by hypothesis, so IsSMulRegular.of_injective makes it regular on the former. This closes the strong induction. The exponent-one case is immediate.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 07DV (lemma-regular-sequence-powers), proof ('Conversely, suppose that f_1^e, f_2, ..., f_r is an M-regular sequence ... by Lemma 07JW ... If r > 2 ... and so on'; the 'and so on' is written out as the induction on i)

proof.text: Conclusion. By induction on $r$ we show, for every $R$-module $N$: $f_1,\dots,f_r$ is weakly $N$-regular iff $f_1^{e_1},\dots,f_r^{e_r}$ is. For $r=0$ both hold. For $r\ge1$, by Step 1, $f_1,\dots,f_r$ is weakly $N$-regular iff $f_1$ is a nonzerodivisor on $N$ and $f_2,\dots,f_r$ is weakly $N/f_1N$-regular; by the induction hypothesis for the module $N/f_1N$ the latter is equivalent to $f_2^{e_2},\dots,f_r^{e_r}$ being weakly $N/f_1N$-regular; when $f_1$ is a nonzerodivisor on $N$ this is equivalent by Steps 4 and 5 (with $f=f_1$, $e=e_1$) to $f_2^{e_2},\dots,f_r^{e_r}$ being weakly $N/f_1^{e_1}N$-regular; and $f_1$ is a nonzerodivisor on $N$ iff $f_1^{e_1}$ is (Step 2(a)). By Step 1 again the result is equivalent to $f_1^{e_1},\dots,f_r^{e_r}$ being weakly $N$-regular. Taking $N=M$ and combining with Step 3 and the first part of Step 1 ($M$-regular = weakly $M$-regular plus nonvanishing of the quotient) gives the lemma for [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence].
